1. What SutraFlow is

SutraFlow is a visual integration designer and engine. You build a Sutra by dragging activities from palettes onto a canvas and connecting them; you map data from earlier activities into later ones; you test and debug it in the studio; and you deploy it to run on the server: on a schedule, when a file or message arrives, or as a REST or SOAP API protected by a security policy and TLS.

One program contains three parts:

  • The studio at http://127.0.0.1:4800: the Designer, Runs, Resources and Server & APIs screens.
  • The engine, which runs Sutras step by step and saves each finished step, so runs survive a restart and long waits cost nothing.
  • The gateway on ports 8080 (HTTP) and 8443 (HTTPS), which serves deployed APIs, separately from the studio.
Words used in this guide

A project holds Sutras, shared resources (connections), schemas and variables. A Sutra is one process diagram. An activity is one box on it; a step is one execution of an activity in a run; a run is one execution of a Sutra. Sutra variables live for one run, Project variables are shared by a project's Sutras, and Sengine variables are server settings made by the administrator.

2. Install and start the server

SutraFlow needs Node.js 22.13 or later; version 24 is recommended. Nothing else is installed: the database is SQLite, built into Node.

Procedure

  1. Open a terminal in the SutraFlow folder.
  2. Install and build: bin/sutraflow setup (Windows: bin\sutraflow.cmd setup). It runs npm install and npm run build, and makes sutraflow.env, where the ports, the data folder and the database are set.
  3. Start: bin/sutraflow start
  4. Open the designer: bin/sutraflow open (http://127.0.0.1:4800). The first time, create the administrator account.

The sutraflow command

Every way of running SutraFlow uses one launcher: bin/sutraflow on Linux and macOS, bin\sutraflow.cmd on Windows (after npm install -g it is simply sutraflow). Its settings come from sutraflow.env in the SutraFlow folder, made from sutraflow.env.example on first use.

CommandWhat it does
start, start engineStarts the studio, or a headless engine beside it on the same database, in the background (output in <data>/logs). --foreground keeps it in the terminal, for services and Laragon.
stop, stop engine, stop allGraceful: no new work, running steps finish first. --force ends a process that does not stop.
restart, status, logs [--follow]Restart; whether each part is ready, its process, addresses and database; the output log.
open [designer|admin|guide|architecture]Opens the page in the browser.
cli ...The sutra command against this studio with the local admin token, for example sutraflow cli sutras list.
db info, db copy --to ...Which database is in use; copies the data to PostgreSQL.
serviceStarting with the machine: a systemd unit on Linux, a scheduled task on Windows.
docker up|down|status|logs|build, docker cluster up|down|...The studio and an engine in Docker, or PostgreSQL with a studio and two engines. Missing passwords and the master key are made once into .env.

For development with automatic reload, run npm run dev and open http://localhost:5173. The tests run with npm test.

Guidelines

Back up the data folder, and above all data/master.key: without it the encrypted secrets cannot be read.
Keep the studio on 127.0.0.1. Publish APIs through the gateway ports, not the studio port.

Server settings

Environment variableDefaultMeaning
SUTRA_DATA_DIR./dataDatabase, master key, deployment config files.
SUTRA_MASTER_KEYthe key fileThe vault key, 32 bytes in base64.
SUTRA_ADMIN_HOST, SUTRA_ADMIN_PORT127.0.0.1, 4800Where the studio listens.
SUTRA_GATEWAY_HTTP_PORT, SUTRA_GATEWAY_HTTPS_PORT8080, 8443Gateway ports until changed in Server & APIs.
SUTRA_WORKERS16Steps that run at the same time.
SUTRA_MAX_STEPS10000Safety limit of steps per run.
SUTRA_REPLY_TIMEOUT_MS60000How long an API caller waits for the reply step.
SUTRA_DBSQLite in the data folderpostgres://user:pass@host/db to keep everything in PostgreSQL.
SUTRA_ENVIRONMENTdevelopment (studio), production (headless engine)What the server is for: development, test or production. Shown on every log line and audit entry; on production only administrators clear project logs.

A development machine on Windows: Laragon

For development and proofs of concept on Windows, Laragon is a convenient base: one installer brings Apache, MySQL, PostgreSQL, PHP, Node.js and HeidiSQL, starts them from one window, and keeps everything under C:\laragon. The DB Ops samples use its MySQL as it comes (127.0.0.1:3306, user root, no password), and SutraFlow itself can keep its data in its PostgreSQL.

  1. Install Laragon (the full edition) and click Start All.
  2. Put SutraFlow in C:\laragon\www\sutra and copy deploy/laragon/sutraflow.env beside it: studio on 4810 (gateway 8090), engine on 4811 (gateway 8091), data in C:\laragon\data\sutraflow outside the web folder. Every command is the launcher: bin\sutraflow.cmd start, stop, status, cli sutras list and so on.
  3. Let Laragon start it: Menu > Procfile, add SutraFlow: autorun C:\laragon\www\sutra\bin\sutraflow.cmd start --foreground PWD=www/sutra.
  4. To use PostgreSQL instead of SQLite, run bin\sutraflow.cmd stop all, then bin\sutraflow.cmd db copy --to postgres://postgres@127.0.0.1:5432/sutraflow (the database is created when missing), and set the same address as SUTRA_DB in sutraflow.env. bin\sutraflow.cmd db info shows which database is in use.

HeidiSQL and PostgreSQL

HeidiSQL needs the PostgreSQL client library to open a PostgreSQL session; without it the connection fails with a missing libpq.dll. Either choose the library in the session's Library field from C:\laragon\bin\postgresql\<version>\bin\libpq.dll, or copy libpq.dll with the libcrypto-*.dll, libssl-*.dll (and, when present, libiconv-*.dll and libintl-*.dll) from that folder into C:\laragon\bin\heidisql and restart HeidiSQL. pgAdmin and DBeaver bring their own drivers, if you prefer them.

pgvector: knowledge bases in PostgreSQL

A knowledge base stored in PostgreSQL (pgvector) needs the pgvector extension in the server. Laragon's PostgreSQL does not include it; add a Windows build that matches the major version of your PostgreSQL:

  1. Find the version: in Laragon's terminal run postgres -V (for example 18).
  2. Download a Windows x64 build of pgvector for that version. pgvector itself publishes source only; community builds exist (for example the pgvector_pgsql_windows releases on GitHub). Use one you trust, for the same PostgreSQL major version and 64-bit.
  3. Stop PostgreSQL in Laragon.
  4. From the zip, copy lib\vector.dll into C:\laragon\bin\postgresql\<version>\lib\, and every file of share\extension\ (vector.control and the vector--*.sql files) into C:\laragon\bin\postgresql\<version>\share\extension\.
  5. Start PostgreSQL again.
  6. Check it: SELECT name, default_version FROM pg_available_extensions WHERE name = 'vector'; returns a row.

SutraFlow then turns the extension on in the knowledge base's database by itself (CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector) the first time a document is added, when its database user may do so (the postgres user can). With a user without that right, run CREATE EXTENSION vector; once in that database as an administrator; SELECT extname, extversion FROM pg_extension WHERE extname = 'vector'; confirms it. Without pgvector, use the built-in or folder store, which need nothing else.

A development machine on Linux

Laragon is for Windows only. On Linux the same set comes from the distribution's packages, or from Docker:

PartDebian / UbuntuFedora / RHEL
Node.js 24Through nvm (nvm install 24), or the NodeSource packages.
MySQL or MariaDBsudo apt install mariadb-serversudo dnf install mariadb-server
PostgreSQLsudo apt install postgresql (newer versions from the PostgreSQL apt repository)sudo dnf install postgresql-server, then sudo postgresql-setup --initdb
pgvectorsudo apt install postgresql-<version>-pgvector from the PostgreSQL apt repository, for example postgresql-17-pgvectorsudo dnf install pgvector_<version> from the PostgreSQL yum repository
A database toolDBeaver, pgAdmin, or the psql and mysql command lines.

With Docker, one command gives PostgreSQL with pgvector already in it: docker run -d --name sutra-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev -p 5432:5432 pgvector/pgvector:pg17, and docker run -d --name sutra-mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=dev -p 3306:3306 mysql:8.4 adds MySQL. Then:

  1. Install SutraFlow (Procedure above: bin/sutraflow setup), and set SUTRA_DATA_DIR in sutraflow.env, for example /home/me/sutraflow-data.
  2. To keep SutraFlow in PostgreSQL: bin/sutraflow db copy --to postgres://postgres:dev@127.0.0.1:5432/sutraflow, then set SUTRA_DB to the same address in sutraflow.env and bin/sutraflow start.
  3. Start it with the machine: bin/sutraflow service prints a systemd unit to install.
  4. Check pgvector as on Windows: SELECT name, default_version FROM pg_available_extensions WHERE name = 'vector';
Guidelines

Laragon and these Linux set-ups are for development machines. For servers, run SutraFlow as a service or in Docker with a managed PostgreSQL (see Running in production).
Keep the master key safe: the file master.key in the data folder (made the first time a secret is saved), or SUTRA_MASTER_KEY. Moving to PostgreSQL copies the encrypted secrets, and only this key opens them.

3. The studio, screen by screen

The top bar holds the four screens, the version in the middle, Admin Console (deployed projects, engines, gateway, users and audit, in its own page), Guide (this guide in a new tab), the light/dark switch and Sign out.

ScreenWhat it is for
DesignerBuilding, testing, debugging and deploying Sutras. Left: the Project explorer and the Palettes. Middle: the canvas and its toolbar. Right: the selected activity's General, Input, Output and Settings tabs.
RunsEvery run with its status, steps, inputs and outputs, logs; approvals waiting for a person.
ResourcesShared connections and security of the current project, and the secrets vault.
Server & APIsExposed services, Sengine variables, gateway ports, TLS certificate, active listeners.

The Designer toolbar

  • Sutra list: opens another Sutra of the project.
  • + New Sutra: a blank Sutra or a starter (REST API, SOAP service, approval with timer).
  • ▶ Test: runs the current draft once with the trigger's test data, without deploying.
  • Debug: runs the draft one activity at a time (see Testing and debugging).
  • ↶ Undo and ↷ Redo (Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y or Ctrl+Shift+Z): step back and forward through your changes to the Sutra, up to 100 of them, such as a deleted activity or connection, a move or a changed mapping. While you type in a field, Ctrl+Z undoes the typing in that field instead.
  • Deploy: makes the current draft the live version.
  • Status badges: Saved, Deployed v2 or Draft only, and the last test result.

The Delete key deletes the selected activity or connection (Backspace does not, so editing text never removes an activity). Changes save automatically. Zoom with the wheel or the + and − buttons; the small map at the bottom left shows where you are.

4. Projects and the explorer

Open the Project tab on the left of the Designer. The project list at the top switches projects; + creates one, starting from:

  • Empty: a name, nothing else.
  • Samples: the sample Sutras you choose. Type in the search box (each word must start a word of the sample, so AI finds the AI samples) and use Select shown; nothing is chosen until you choose.
  • Package file: chosen Sutras of a .sutra package from any SutraFlow server, with the project's connections, schemas and variables. They come in as drafts, so nothing starts and no address clashes with the original; tick Deploy the Sutras that are deployed in the package to deploy them as well. Secret values never travel: the import tells you which secrets to add.
  • Copy a project: chosen Sutras of a project on this server, as drafts in a new project. The original is not changed. Good for a proof of concept or a study copy.

Each project holds:

SectionWhat it holds
SutrasThe Sutras, with their deployed version. Each Sutra also has Sutra variables, read as {vars.name}.
ResourcesThe project's connections and security, each listed under the name you gave it with a symbol for its kind. + opens the list of kinds: HTTP connection, Outbound security, API security policy, AI provider, Email (SMTP and IMAP), Database, Kafka, RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, Firebase, OAuth connection. The name is its key in the deployment config, so you can rename it safely.
SchemasShared JSON (JSON Schema or a sample document) and XML (XSD) schemas. Activities pick them to describe payloads, bodies, CSV rows and mapping targets.
Service descriptorsWSDL files that Invoke SOAP service can call.
ConfigurationProject variables, the deployment config and the log file settings.

Folders

Sutras, Resources, Schemas and Service descriptors can each sit in folders, and folders in folders, so a large project stays tidy. Each section has its own folders. Folders only arrange the explorer: a name is still unique in the project, and deploying, calling and packages work as before.

  • + Folder under the list makes a folder; type Orders/Inbound for one inside another.
  • Drag a Sutra or a folder onto a folder to move it there, or onto the line Drag here for the top level.
  • The ⋯ button beside a Sutra moves it by typing or picking a folder. Beside a folder it renames or moves the folder with everything in it, makes a folder inside, or removes the folder. Removing a folder never deletes Sutras: they move up one level.
  • A new Sutra goes in the folder of the Sutra open at the time.
  • Samples go to Samples/<topic>, for example Samples/SQL and Samples/REST and microservices, and the connections made for them to Resources > Samples. Samples added before folders existed were filed there once, when the server was updated. Move them anywhere afterwards.
  • Packages and project copies keep each item's folder.
  • Importing chosen Sutras (a new project from a package or a copy) brings the connections, schemas and service descriptors those Sutras use, directly or through each other (an MCP server and its policy), in their folders, and nothing else.

Project log

Configuration > Project log shows what this project's runs wrote to its log file (set it up under Logging), newest at the bottom. Filter by level, by Runs from (deployed Sutras or designer tests) and by words; refresh it every 5 seconds; download what is shown. Every line carries two tags: the server it ran on (production, test, development) and the run, deployed v3 for a deployed Sutra and its version, or editor test / editor debug for the designer's own runs. In the file a line reads 2026-10-19T09:12:03Z INFO {development, editor test} [Orders / 3f2a91c0 / Check stock] ....

Clear log empties the file and its rotated copies; Clear test runs deletes the finished test and debug runs of the project and keeps deployed runs. Developers may do both on development and test servers; on a production server only an administrator may. Both are recorded in the audit log.

Missing project variables

When a step reads a project variable the project does not define ({{gv.X}}, {gv.X}, $gv.X in JSONata or get-project-variable('X')), the activity shows ⚠ on the canvas and a warning at the top of its tabs, and it reads as empty while running. The same warning shows on a connection that reads one, and on every step that uses that connection. Add to project variables adds the missing names; give them values under Configuration > Project variables. Deploy lists the same warnings.

Add a connection

  1. Next to Resources, click + and choose the kind, for example HTTP connection.
  2. Give it your own name, such as Orders API. The explorer lists it under that name.
  3. Fill in its settings: address and port, user, the vault secret for the password. Settings marked {x} take a project variable, such as {{gv.ORDERS_URL}}, so each environment can use its own value.
  4. Click Test connection. SutraFlow tries the settings as they are on screen, with variables filled in, and says what happened: the HTTP status, the database it reached, the mailbox count, the AI model that answered.
  5. Click Save.

Add a shared schema

  1. Next to Schemas, click +.
  2. Give it a name and choose the type: JSON or XML (XSD).
  3. Paste the content, or load a file. A JSON sample document is enough; SutraFlow works out the fields.
  4. For an XSD with several root elements, choose the default root element.
  5. Save. The Fields tree shows the result: * marks a required field, ** a repeating one.

5. Building a Sutra

  1. Click + New Sutra and choose a starter, or start blank.
  2. Drag a trigger from the Triggers palette (or keep Manual start). A Sutra has one trigger.
  3. Drag activities onto the canvas. Search the palettes with the box at the top.
  4. Connect an activity's output (a circle on its right) to the next activity's input (on its left). Activities with several outputs, such as If / else or Router, have one circle per output.
  5. Select each activity and fill in its tabs.
  6. Click Test. Each activity shows its result; select one and open Output to see the values.
  7. When it works, click Deploy.

Branches, errors and ends

  • Every activity except triggers and End has a red error output. Connect it to handle a failure; otherwise the failure ends the run as failed.
  • A branch that is not taken is skipped; a Merge after it still continues.
  • End ends a branch. With Sutra: success or Sutra: error it stops the whole Sutra at once and cancels the other branches.
  • Throw error fails a branch with your message, so an error output before it can handle it.
  • The Error handler activity catches every error whose activity has no error output connected: one place to log, alert and clean up.

Connections: names and conditions

Click a connection to name it and decide when it is taken. The name and condition show on the canvas.

TakenMeaning
AlwaysEvery time the activity finishes on that output. The default.
When a condition is trueA formula on the previous activity's output, which it reads as {input.x}; for example ={input.amount} > 1000 named Order > 1000. Several "when" connections can be taken together.
OtherwiseTaken when none of the "when" connections from the same output was taken.

A connection that is not taken counts as a skipped branch, so a Merge after it still continues. For many routes, or for routes on the same message used in several places, a Router activity keeps them in one place.

Sample Sutras

Samples that need a connection get one in the project, named Sample ... (Sample MySQL, Sample SFTP, Sample SMTP and so on), already chosen in their activities. Fill in its address, user and password, click Test connection, and the sample runs. Adding more samples later reuses these connections. The SQL samples use Laragon's MySQL defaults (127.0.0.1:3306, user root, no password).

Click + New Sutra, then Choose samples to tick the ones you want, or Add all. Test each one and open its activities' Input and Output tabs to see how it is built. Samples that write files use C:/sutra/samples; change the folder to suit your machine.

Reusable Sutras

Put logic used in several places in its own Sutra: a Manual start with a payload schema, the steps, and Return with the result. Other Sutras run it with Call Sutra, wait for the result and continue; a failure inside it arrives on Call Sutra's error output. While you test, the draft of the called Sutra runs; deployed Sutras call its deployed version.

Loops

Any activity can run more than once (Settings tab → Loop):

  • For each item of a list: once per item of Loop over. Map {iteration.value} (or {item}) and {iteration.index}; the mapper lists them under $iteration. The output is iterations (every result) and count.
  • Repeat while a condition holds: runs, then checks the condition, for example ={iteration.output.status} != 'DONE', with a delay between runs: polling until a job is finished. The output is the last result plus _iterations.

A looping activity shows ↻ after its type on the canvas. Each loop has a maximum number of runs (1000 by default).

Sutras working together

  • Call Sutra: run another Sutra and use its result.
  • Send to channel and Channel trigger: tell other deployed Sutras that something happened, in memory.
  • Counter: a number shared by all runs of the project, such as a sequence or a daily total.
Guidelines

Name activities by what they do (Get order, not HTTP 1): mappings refer to activities by name, and renaming one updates them.
Give every API branch a reply, including the error branches.

6. The activity tabs

TabWhat it holds
GeneralThe activity's name and its fixed settings: folders, URLs, methods, connections, formats. Fields with {x} accept project and Sengine variables ({{gv.OUTBOX}}, {{ev.REGION}}) and = formulas. Map inputs opens the Input tab.
InputThe mapper: values that come from earlier activities (see Mapping data).
OutputThe fields this activity produces, before any run; after a run, the values it received and produced.
SettingsRetries with a growing delay, a timeout, a breakpoint for debugging, and skip this activity.

Settings tab reference

SettingWhat it doesDefault
Retries on failureRuns the activity again after a failure, up to this many times (at most 20), before the error output is used.0
First retry delay (ms)Wait before the first retry; each retry waits twice as long as the one before.1000
Timeout (ms)Fails the activity if it takes longer.120000
Skip this activityPasses the input through without running the activity.off
BreakpointThe debugger pauses before this activity.off
LoopRun once, for each item of a list, or repeat while a condition holds (see Loops).Run once
Loop over / Repeat whileThe list, or the condition checked after each run.—
Delay between runs (ms)Wait between two runs of the loop.0
Maximum runsFails the activity when the loop would run more often (at most 10000).1000

7. Mapping data

Select an activity and open Input. Sutra Data on the left lists everything the activity can use: $_projectVariables, $_sengineVariables (read only), $_sutraContext (this run: id, name, version, step), $_sutraVariables, the previous step as input, and every earlier activity by name. Activity Input on the right lists what the activity needs; for structured inputs, the tree of the chosen schema.

Procedure

  1. Drag a field from the left onto a target field on the right. A line shows the link.
  2. Or select a target and write its formula in the box below. Click a function in the library to insert it; the preview under the box shows the result against the last test run.
  3. Drop a list onto a repeating target: a For-Each is created and fields with the same names are mapped. Inside it, {item.x} is the current row and {index} its position.
  4. Click Auto map to map every field that has the same name on both sides.
  5. Click any field, on either side, to highlight where it is mapped; other lines fade.

For-Each, If and Choose

  • Where keeps only rows where a condition holds, using the row's own column names: upper-case(Country) = 'INDIA'.
  • Group by makes one element per distinct value; inside, {group.key}, {group.items} and {group.count}.
  • Sort by orders the rows, ascending or descending.
  • If includes the target only when its condition is true.
  • Choose takes the first When whose condition is true, otherwise the Otherwise value.

Formulas

A formula starts with = in a plain field, and is implied in mapping targets. References are written in braces: {input.name}, {nodes.Get order.body.id}, {gv.OUTBOX}, {vars.total}.

=concat('Name : ', {input.name})
=upper-case(substring-before({input.email}, '@'))
=format-date('DD-MM-YY', {nodes.Parse XML.Order.date})
=format-dateTime('DD MMM YYYY HH:mm', current-dateTime(), 'Asia/Kolkata')
=string-to-base64(concat({gv.USER}, ':', {gv.PASSWORD}))
=if({input.amount} > 1000, 'bulk', 'retail')
={input.rows}[upper-case(Country) = 'INDIA']        rows where the condition holds
=count({input.rows}[Amount > 1000])
={input.rows}[1].City                                  first row, then a field
=xs:integer({input.qty})
=concat({gv.OUT}, '\', current-timestamp('YYYYMMDD'), '.csv')
=set-project-variable('LAST_RUN', current-dateTime())

Backslashes in quoted text are literal, so Windows paths need no escaping. Write a quote twice to include it: 'O''Brien'. Function names ignore case. Every function is listed in Function reference.

Templates in text fields

Text fields such as an email body or a log message use {{ }} templates with pipes: Order {{input.id | upper}} for {{input.amount | number:2}}. The pipes are listed in Template pipes.

When to use JSONata instead

For heavy reshaping of repeating JSON (filter, group, total and nest in one go) a single [[jsonata

activity is often clearer than many mapper rules.]]

8. Schemas and WSDLs

Activities that receive or produce structured data let you pick a shared schema: Manual start (payload), REST service (request body), Send HTTP request (body and response), Map data (target), Parse/Render JSON and XML, the file activities (CSV row schema), Invoke SOAP service (arguments and response).

  • With a schema, later activities see the fields in the mapper before any run, with types and repeating markers.
  • Without one, SutraFlow infers the fields from the test data or the first run.
  • Activities keep their standard fields when a schema is chosen: for example Read file still returns the file name, path and size next to the rows, and Write file always returns the written file's details.

An XSD with several global elements is chosen as Schema::Element. A WSDL added under Service descriptors appears in Invoke SOAP service, which lists its services, ports and operations.

9. Variables and the deployment config

KindRead asSet whereLifetime
Sutra variables{vars.name}Sutra properties; Set variablesOne run.
Project variables{gv.NAME}, {{gv.NAME}}, get-project-variable('NAME')Project → Configuration; the deployment config; set-project-variableKept; a value set at run time lasts until the server restarts or the config changes.
Sengine variables{ev.NAME}, {{ev.NAME}}, get-sengine-variable('NAME')Server & APIs (administrator)Kept; shared by every project on the server. Sutras read them only.

Project variables have a type: string, number, boolean or secret. A secret variable holds the name of a vault secret, never the value.

Read Sengine variables, do not change them

Sengine variables are mostly engine settings (a region, a data centre, a shared folder) that every project relies on. Read them in Sutras; change them only in Server & APIs. set-sengine-variable works only when the administrator ticks Allow Sutras to change Sengine variables, and one Sutra could then change the behaviour of every project.

The deployment config file

Operations staff change settings per environment without opening the studio. The deployment config holds overrides for project variables, resource settings (hosts, ports, URLs, queue names) and logging. Export it from the project, edit it, and import it, or place it at data/config/<project>.json.

{
  "variables": { "OUTBOX": "D:\\exports", "API_BASE": "${env:ORDERS_API:-https://test.example.com}" },
  "resources": { "Orders DB": { "host": "${env:DB_HOST}", "port": 5432 } },
  "logging":   { "path": "D:\\logs\\orders.log", "level": "info" }
}

${env:NAME} reads an environment variable of the server; ${env:NAME:-default} gives a default.

Logging

Each project writes its own log file: path, level, text or JSON lines, rotation by size, and optionally each step's input and output. Set it under Configuration or in the deployment config.

10. Testing and debugging

Test runs the draft once with the trigger's test data. Each activity shows a status dot; select one and open Output to read what it received and produced. API triggers use their test request, message and file triggers their test message or event.

Debug runs the draft one activity at a time:

  1. Optionally set breakpoints: Settings tab → Breakpoint: pause here when debugging.
  2. Click Debug. The run pauses before the first activity. The canvas outlines it, and its Output tab shows the input it will receive.
  3. Step runs that activity and pauses before the next. Continue runs to the next breakpoint. Pause stops before the next activity. Stop cancels the run.

Runs

The Runs screen lists every run: Sutra, version, trigger, status, time. Open one to see each step with its input, output, time and error, and the run log. Approvals lists runs waiting for a person.

11. Deploying and versions

The Sutra you edit is a draft. Deploy saves it as the next version (v1, v2, ...) and makes it live: its timer, file, email, message or Drive trigger starts listening, and its REST or SOAP service is published on the gateway.

  • Runs already in progress finish on the version they started with.
  • Editing after a deploy changes only the draft until you deploy again.
  • Other systems start a deployed Sutra with the Run API: POST /api/flows/{flowId}/run?wait=30000 with { "input": { ... } }.

12. Exposing APIs: security and TLS

A REST service or SOAP service trigger publishes the Sutra on the gateway. Server & APIs lists every exposed service with its addresses and security policy.

API security policy

Create a policy in Resources → API security policy and pick it on the trigger. It checks, in order: HTTPS required, IP allow list (addresses or IPv4 ranges), caller authentication, then a rate limit per caller. CORS origins are optional.

AuthenticationHow callers prove who they are
NoneOpen to anyone. For testing only.
BasicUser name and password; passwords are vault secrets.
API keyA key in a header; keys are vault secrets.
JWT bearerA signed token, checked with a JWKS URL, a public key or a shared secret; issuer, audience and scopes.
WS-Security UsernameTokenSOAP only; password digest with a time window and replay protection.
Mutual TLSA client certificate signed by the client CA set in Server & APIs; optionally only listed subjects.

TLS certificate of the gateway

  • Self-signed: for testing.
  • Own certificate: paste the PEM chain and key; the key is checked against the certificate and stored encrypted.
  • Let's Encrypt: enter the domains and an email. The gateway's HTTP port must be reachable as port 80 on each domain. Start with staging; certificates renew 30 days before they expire, without dropping connections.
  • Client CA: enables mutual TLS for policies that use it.

TLS 1.2 is the minimum.

13. Calling services: REST, SOAP and WS-Security

Outbound calls take two shared resources:

  • HTTP connection: base URL, timeout, default headers, certificate checking, extra trusted CAs, client certificate and key for mutual TLS, proxy.
  • Outbound security: how SutraFlow proves who it is.

Circuit breaker

When a service is down, waiting for every call to time out slows every run. On the HTTP connection, set Open the circuit after to a number of failures in a row (errors or 5xx replies). The circuit then opens: calls through that connection fail at once with "Circuit open" for the time you set, then one trial call decides whether it closes again. SOAP faults do not count; they mean the service is up. Combine it with retries and an error output that, for example, queues the work for later.

MethodForWhat is sent
BasicREST, SOAPAuthorization: Basic
BearerREST, SOAPAuthorization: Bearer
API keyREST, SOAPA header or query parameter.
OAuth 2.0 client credentialsREST, SOAPA token from the token URL, cached until it expires.
Custom headersREST, SOAPAny headers; values may use {{secret.X}}.
WS-Security UsernameTokenSOAPPassword digest (nonce and created) or text, optional timestamp.
WS-Security SAML tokenSOAPA SAML 1.1 or 2.0 assertion from the vault or from an earlier step (for example a token service call).
WS-Security X.509SOAPA binary security token and an XML signature over Body and Timestamp.

See Send HTTP request and Invoke SOAP service.

14. Messaging: Kafka, RabbitMQ and ActiveMQ

The Service Bus palette works the JMS way: Publish message sends, Message subscriber starts a run per message, and Confirm message acknowledges at a point you choose.

  • Put queue and topic names in project variables ({{gv.ORDER_QUEUE}}) so each environment can use its own.
  • JMS headers: delivery mode (persistent or not), priority, time to live, message id, correlation id, reply-to and type; plus your own properties.
  • Acknowledgement: auto on receipt, client after the run succeeds, explicit with Confirm message. On failure: requeue, or send to the dead-letter queue after a number of redeliveries.

15. Files

File activities read and write text, CSV rows, lines, JSON, XML and binary (base64) in UTF-8, UTF-16, ISO-8859-1, Windows-1252 and other encodings.

  • With a row schema, CSV and lines become typed, repeating rows, ready for a For-Each in the mapper.
  • List / read directory takes wildcards: C:\in\*.csv, or =concat({gv.DIR}, '\*.csv').
  • Write file appends or overwrites, and always returns the file's name, path, size and what it did.
  • File trigger reacts to added, modified and removed files; move processed files away with Move / copy / delete file.

SFTP and FTP servers

The SFTP / FTP palette works with files on another server: Remote file trigger, List remote files, Read remote file, Write remote file and Move / copy / delete remote file. Each step names the protocol and an SFTP server or FTP server connection.

  • SFTP signs in with a password or a private key from the vault. Paste the server's host key fingerprint (Test connection shows it, as SHA256:...) so a different server is refused.
  • FTP uses explicit TLS (FTPS) by default; implicit TLS and plain FTP are there for old servers.
  • The base folder fences the steps in: a path such as ../../etc is refused.

Time limits for slow or far-away servers

A server in another region, or a busy one, can take a while to answer. Each SFTP or FTP connection has its own limits:

SettingDefaultWhat it limits
Connect time limit30 sReaching the server and signing in.
Response time limit60 sEach operation: a listing, a read, a write, a rename. A large file is one operation, so allow for its transfer time.
Connection attempts3Tries after a network failure. A wrong password or host key is not tried again.
Wait between attempts5 sThe pause before the next try.
Keep-alive every15 sSFTP only: keeps a slow session open through firewalls. 0 turns it off.

The step itself has a time limit too, in its Settings tab. SFTP and FTP steps and every AI activity allow 10 minutes by default (other activities 2 minutes); raise it for very large files or slow models. When a limit is passed, the error says which one, for example Reading inbox/big.csv took longer than 60 s (Response time limit of the connection).

16. Databases, email, Firebase and apps

  • DB Ops works with PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle and SQLite. Parameters are written :name and are always bound, never pasted into the SQL. SQL script runs install scripts (tables, procedures, seed rows); a REST service with Call procedure then turns a stored procedure into a microservice, as Sample: Procedure as a microservice shows.
  • Email: SMTP to send, IMAP to start a run per incoming message.
  • Firebase: Firestore, Realtime Database and push notifications, with a service-account key held in the vault.
  • Apps (Google Sheets, Drive and Docs, Dropbox, YouTube, Facebook Pages) use an OAuth connection: create it in Resources, then click Connect account and sign in once. Tokens are stored in the vault and refreshed automatically. Connected API call reaches any other API of the same account.

17. Custom code, HTML and AI

  • JavaScript code runs your JavaScript in a sandbox without host access, with time and memory limits.
  • HTML template builds HTML with escaped placeholders, loops and conditions.
  • Transform (JSONata) transforms JSON with one expression.
  • The Scripts palette runs PowerShell script, Shell script (bash, sh or cmd) and Run program on the server, capturing the output, the error output and the exit code. An administrator must allow scripts in Server & APIs first; values reach scripts as environment variables, never as script text.
  • The AI palette: AI prompt, AI classify, AI router, AI extract, AI summarize, AI translate and AI sentiment. Each also returns ai: the provider, engine, model, input, output and total tokens, and the time taken.

AI providers

An AI provider connection chooses the engine. Several can exist side by side, for example a fast one for routing and a strong one for summaries.

EngineWhat it needsDefault model
Claude APIAn Anthropic API key in the vault.claude-opus-5-5; also claude-sonnet-5-5, claude-haiku-5-5
Gemini APIA Google AI Studio or Vertex API key.gemini-3-pro-preview; also other Gemini 3 models
OpenAI APIAn OpenAI API key. Any compatible server works with its own API base URL.gpt-5
OllamaAn Ollama server; on this machine by default (http://127.0.0.1:11434). A full endpoint such as http://localhost:11434/api/generate also works, and the Ollama API setting chooses chat or generate. No key; nothing leaves your network, so it works offline.The first model installed, or the one you pick
LM StudioLM Studio's local server (http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1).The model loaded in LM Studio
Hugging FaceA Hugging Face token; uses Hugging Face Inference Providers.A model id such as Qwen/Qwen3-8B
Hugging Face TGI (local)Text Generation Inference running on your machine (default http://127.0.0.1:8090/v1; SutraFlow's gateway uses 8080).The model TGI serves
OpenAI-compatible serverAny server with the OpenAI chat API: llama.cpp, vLLM, LocalAI, Jan. Key only when the server asks for one.The server's first model, or the one you pick
Claude CLI, Gemini CLI, OpenAI Codex CLIThe command-line tool installed and signed in on the server (claude, gemini, codex). Uses that tool's own account.The tool's default, or the one you set

Click List models to see the models the engine offers and pick one; Test connection shows which model answered, with tokens and time.

Adding models to Ollama, online or offline

  • Pull a model by name, such as qwen3, when the Ollama machine has internet.
  • Import from a path on this server when it does not. Copy the files over (USB drive, share), then give their path: a .gguf file; a Modelfile (FROM file.gguf, with TEMPLATE, SYSTEM and PARAMETER); a Safetensors model folder; or an Ollama models folder copied from another machine (it holds manifests and blobs), with the model to take from it. SutraFlow sends the files to Ollama through its API and registers them under the name you choose.

One setting per environment

The deployment config overrides any connection setting, the engine included. Test with a local Ollama and run production on another engine without changing a Sutra:

"resources": { "AI provider": { "engine": "Claude API", "model": "claude-sonnet-5-5", "apiKeySecret": "ANTHROPIC_KEY" } }
Command-line tools

The prompt is sent to the tool on standard input, never on the command line, and the tool runs in an empty folder as the SutraFlow server user. Keep the tool's own permissions for running commands and editing files switched off: a message from outside could otherwise ask it to act on the server.

Guidelines

Route AI decisions that matter (money, customers) through [[approval

until you trust them.]]

18. AI skills over MCP

A Sutra that starts with an AI tool trigger is a skill: AI assistants such as Claude connect to SutraFlow over the Model Context Protocol (MCP), see the skills, and call them. Each call runs the Sutra with the arguments the AI chose, and Reply to AI sends the outcome back. Skills can do anything a Sutra does: write a CSV file, post to a Facebook page, look up an order in a database, start an approval.

Build a skill

  1. Under Resources, add an MCP server: its address on the gateway (for example /mcp/orders), a title, instructions for the AI, and an API security policy. One server holds many skills.
  2. Create a Sutra that starts with MCP skill, choose the server, and describe the tool: name, title, what it does and when to use it, and its inputs.
  3. Build the work, and end every branch with Reply to AI; on error branches tick Is an error.
  4. Test it in the studio with the trigger's test arguments, then Deploy. Server & APIs lists each skill with its address.

Connect an assistant

Give the assistant the server's address and, when a policy is set, the key or token as a header. With Claude Code:

claude mcp add --transport http orders https://your-server:8443/mcp/orders --header "X-API-Key: your-key"

Other assistants that support MCP over HTTP take the same address and header. Skills without a server are at /mcp.

Sample skills

Add sample Sutras also adds an MCP server named Sample skills (/mcp/samples) with two skills: Skill: Write CSV file and Skill: Post to Facebook page. Choose a security policy on the server, a Facebook connection and page on the second skill, and deploy them.

Guidelines

Protect every MCP server with an API security policy: a skill acts with the server's rights.
Tick Changes data on skills that create, change or delete something, so the assistant asks the user first.
Write descriptions for someone who has never seen the Sutra: the AI chooses skills by them.

19. AI agents and knowledge bases (RAG)

An AI agent works towards a goal in steps: it thinks, picks a tool, uses it, reads the result, and repeats until it can answer. Its tools are your own Sutras: any Sutra that starts with an AI tool trigger is a tool for the agents of its project. A knowledge base and an outside MCP server add more tools.

Build an agent

  1. Make the tools: Sutras that start with AI tool, describe what they do, and end with Reply to AI. The description is what the agent chooses by.
  2. Under Resources, add an AI memory store (built-in is enough to start) and, for documents, a Knowledge base.
  3. Make the agent Sutra: Agent channel (or any trigger), AI guard, AI agent, and Agent reply on every branch. Connect needs a person to Ask a person.
  4. Test it with the trigger's test message; the Output tab shows each step the agent took.
  5. Deploy the tools and the agent.

Memory and the context window

Every run stands alone, so a conversation lives in the memory store under its session id. Each step sends, in this order: instructions and tools, the running summary, knowledge passages (at most a quarter of the window), the newest turns that still fit, and the message. When the history no longer fits, the oldest turns are folded into the summary. Messages of one session are handled one at a time, in arrival order; other sessions run alongside, and the queue survives restarts.

Where the agent lives

A deployed Sutra with an Agent channel trigger is reachable at once at every entry point you tick:

Entry pointAddressUsed by
Chat page and API/chat/<name>, POST /chat/<name>/api, /chat/<name>/widget.jsPeople; any web page (one script tag adds a chat button)
OpenAI-compatiblePOST /v1/chat/completions with model = nameApps and SDKs that take an OpenAI base address
MCPthe tool ask_<name> on /mcp or your MCP serverClaude, ChatGPT, Copilot, Antigravity, Cursor
A2A/a2a/<name> and its agent cardOther agents

Work that takes longer than Answer within, or waits for a person, answers at once with a job id; the caller fetches the answer later with it (GET /chat/<name>/jobs/<id>, the job argument of the MCP tool, tasks/get in A2A, or the message status <id> in the OpenAI API). The same agent can run on several servers; point them at one PostgreSQL database to share sessions.

Knowledge bases (RAG)

A knowledge base keeps documents as passages with vectors, so agents find them by meaning. Store them built-in or in a folder, or in PostgreSQL with pgvector, Qdrant, Chroma or Pinecone. Vectors come from a model (Ollama nomic-embed-text, OpenAI, Gemini) or, offline, from built-in word vectors.

  • Fill it with a feed Sutra: a source (SharePoint / OneDrive trigger, Google Drive / Docs trigger, File trigger, Remote file trigger, a list of web pages) → Read document text → Add to knowledge. A removed file goes to Remove knowledge.
  • Use it with Ask knowledge (answers only from the documents, with sources), Search knowledge, or an agent with the knowledge base set.
  • Who sees what: store details with each source (for example groups = finance) and filter on them when searching.
Guidelines

Put rules before the agent: route refunds, cancellations and other decisions with an If, not by asking the model to choose.
Give small models few tools and short instructions; they look things up well but may wander.
Protect public entry points with a policy that has a rate limit.

20. Secrets and studio security

  • Passwords, keys and tokens live in the vault (Resources → Secrets), encrypted with AES-256-GCM. Settings hold the secret's name.
  • Secret values are never returned by the API. A secret used in a step is masked in stored outputs and logs.
  • The studio listens on 127.0.0.1 by default. Sessions are HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookies; every change needs a request header that browsers cannot forge across sites; repeated failed sign-ins are slowed down.

21. Releases: packages and the command line

Build in the studio; release a package: one .sutra file with the whole project. It has every deployed Sutra at its version, the connections and API policies (secret names, never secret values), shared schemas and WSDLs, project variables and logging. The same file goes from test to production; each environment keeps its own deployment config and secrets.

In the studio

  1. Open Project → Configuration → Releases (packages).
  2. Give a version, such as 1.4.0, and a note, then Build and download.
  3. On the target server, open the same panel, choose the file, read the check (missing secrets, addresses already used by another project), and Deploy.
  4. The history lists every deployment; Deploy again or Roll back returns to an earlier package.

Deploying matches everything by name. A Sutra whose content changed gets a new version; an unchanged one is left alone, so the same package twice changes nothing. Sutras not in the package are undeployed (kept, not deleted) unless you tick Keep Sutras that are not in the package deployed.

From the command line or a CI pipeline

sutra package  --project "Orders" --version 1.4.0 --out orders-1.4.0.sutra
sutra check    orders-1.4.0.sutra
sutra test     orders-1.4.0.sutra --secrets-from-env
sutra deploy   orders-1.4.0.sutra --server https://engine:4800 --token $TOKEN
sutra rollback --project "Orders" --server https://engine:4800 --token $TOKEN

The token is a system account's API token (Admin Console, System accounts), limited to its roles, or the server's SUTRA_ADMIN_TOKEN. Without --server the tool works on the local data folder. Exit code 0 means success, 1 a failed check, test or deploy, 2 wrong usage. sutra test runs every Sutra of the package with its test data in a throw-away server.

From a Sutra

The Release palette does the same steps inside a Sutra, so a release can itself be a Sutra: on a timer or a REST call, Build package, Deploy package to a test engine, Human approval, Deploy package to production, then Send email the result. Check package and Roll back complete it. These activities are off until an administrator allows them in Server & APIs.

22. Command reference

SutraFlow has two command line tools. Both lists below are read from the tools themselves when this guide is built, so they always match the version you have; sutraflow help and sutra help print the same.

  • sutraflow runs SutraFlow on this machine: install, start, stop, status, logs, Docker. Windows: bin\sutraflow.cmd; Linux and macOS: bin/sutraflow; sutraflow after npm install -g.
  • sutra works with what is in SutraFlow: packages and releases, users, secrets, deployed Sutras, runs, approvals, engines, alerts and the gateway. It works on the data folder directly, or on a running server with --server and --token. sutraflow cli <command> runs it against the local studio, already signed in; on its own it is npm run sutra -- <command> or sutra after npm install -g.

sutraflow: running SutraFlow

CommandWhat it does
sutraflow setupInstalls the packages and builds SutraFlow (from a source folder), and makes sutraflow.env and the local admin token.
sutraflow start [engine] [--foreground]Starts the studio (designer, Admin Console, engine and gateway), or a headless engine beside it on the same database. In the background unless --foreground; its output goes to <data>/logs/<name>.out.log.
sutraflow stop [engine|all] [--force]Stops gracefully: no new work, running steps finish (up to 30 s). --force ends the process when it does not stop in time.
sutraflow restart [engine]Stops, then starts.
sutraflow statusStudio and engine: running or not, ready, addresses, database.
sutraflow logs [engine] [--follow]The last lines of the output log.
sutraflow open [designer|admin|guide|architecture]Opens the page in the browser.
sutraflow cli <sutra command ...>The sutra command, pointed at this studio with the local admin token, for example: sutraflow cli sutras list
sutraflow db info | db copy --to <postgres://...> [--replace]Which database is in use; copies the data to PostgreSQL (stop first).
sutraflow serviceHow to start SutraFlow with the machine (systemd unit or Windows task).
sutraflow docker up | down | status | logs [service] | buildThe studio and an engine in Docker (docker-compose.yml).
sutraflow docker cluster up | down | status | logsPostgreSQL, a studio and two engines (docker-compose.cluster.yml).
sutraflow versionThe SutraFlow version.

Settings: sutraflow.env in the SutraFlow folder (ports, data folder, SUTRA_DB, Node path); SUTRAFLOW_ENV names another file.

sutra: releases, people and operations

CommandWhat it does
Releases
sutra package --project <name> [--version 1.0.0] [--note text] [--sutras "A,B"] [--out file.sutra]Builds a package of a project: every deployed Sutra at its deployed version.
sutra check <file.sutra> [--project <name>]Checks a package against a server: activities, secrets, addresses in use.
sutra deploy <file.sutra> [--project <name>] [--config ops.json] [--keep-others]Deploys a package; Sutras of the project not in it are undeployed unless --keep-others.
sutra test <file.sutra> [--skip "A,B"] [--secret NAME=value ...] [--secrets-from-env]Installs the package in a throw-away server and runs every Sutra with its test data.
sutra history --project <name>Deployments of packages to a project.
sutra rollback --project <name> [--to <id>]Deploys the package before the current one, or the deployment with that id.
Server, data and people
sutra statusServer health, readiness and engines.
sutra secret set <NAME> (--value <v> | --from-env <VAR>)Saves a secret in the vault (encrypted); Sutras and connections use it by name.
sutra db copy --to <postgres://user:pass@host/db | file.db> [--replace]Copies this server's data (SUTRA_DATA_DIR or SUTRA_DB) to another database, for example from SQLite to PostgreSQL. A missing PostgreSQL database is created. Stop the server first; then start it with SUTRA_DB set to the new address and the same master key.
sutra db infoWhich database the server uses, and its row counts.
sutra user add <name> [--role administrator] [--project <name>] [--system] [--display "Name"] [--email e] [--password <p> | --password-from-env <VAR>] [--keep-password]Adds a person (or a system account) with a role for all projects or one project. People choose a new password at their first sign-in unless --keep-password. This is how a headless engine gets its first administrator.
sutra user listPeople and system accounts with their roles.
sutra user password <name> (--password <p> | --password-from-env <VAR>)Sets a new password; the person chooses their own at the next sign-in.
sutra user disable | enable | unlock | sign-out | delete <name>Blocks or allows sign-in, clears a lock after wrong passwords, ends all sessions, or deletes.
Operating deployed Sutras (the same actions as the Admin Console; need --server)
sutra sutras list [--project <name>]Deployed Sutras with their state and runs of the last 24 hours.
sutra sutras start | stop | restart <sutra> --project <name>Starts or stops a deployed Sutra's triggers; restart does both.
sutra sutras deploy <sutra> --project <name> --version <n>Deploys a published version of a Sutra (an earlier one to go back).
sutra sutras tune <sutra> --project <name> [--max-runs n] [--priority n] [--run-timeout-min n] [--retries n] [--retry-delay-ms n] [--step-data all|errors-only|none] [--retention-days n]Tuning of one Sutra: runs at a time, priority, time limit, retries, what runs keep and how long.
sutra runs list [--sutra <name> --project <name>] [--status failed] [--limit 50]Recent runs, newest first.
sutra runs show | resubmit | cancel <run id>One run step by step; runs it again from its failed steps; or cancels it.
sutra approvals list | approve <id> [--comment text] | reject <id> [--comment text]Steps waiting for a person, and the decision on one.
sutra engines list | drain <engine> | housekeepingEngines of the cluster; stops one gracefully; deletes runs and audit entries past retention.
sutra engines tune [--engine <id>] [--workers n] [--max-steps n] [--reply-timeout-ms n] [--retention-days n] [--audit-retention-days n] [--trace-sampling 0..1]Engine tuning, for every engine or one: workers, limits, retention, trace sampling.
sutra token create <system account> [--name text] [--expires-days n] | list <account> | revoke <account> <id>API tokens of a system account, for scripts and pipelines.
sutra audit [--actor name] [--outcome ok|failed|denied] [--from 2026-10-01] [--csv]Who did what, when, and with what outcome.
sutra audit retention [<days>]How long audit entries are kept; with a number, sets it (0 = keep everything).
sutra audit clear --before 2026-10-01 | --older | --allClears audit entries before a date, older than the retention, or all; the clearing is recorded.
Alerts (need --server)
sutra alerts [list | history] | ack <id> | resolve <id> | check | rules | channels | test <channel>Open and past alerts, acknowledging and resolving them, checking now, the rules and channels, and a test message to a channel.
Gateway (apps, keys, plans, firewall, traffic; need --server)
sutra gateway apps | plans | stats [--period 1h|24h|7d|30d] | log [--status errors|refused|ok] [--limit n]Apps, plans, traffic statistics and the request log.
sutra gateway app add <name> [--scopes "orders:read orders:write"] [--plan <name>] [--contact text]Adds an app that calls your APIs, with its scopes and plan.
sutra gateway app disable | enable | delete <name>Blocks, allows or deletes an app.
sutra gateway key create <app> [--name text] [--expires-days n] | key revoke <app> <key id>Makes an API key for an app (shown once) or revokes one.
sutra gateway plan set <name> [--per-minute n] [--per-hour n] [--per-day n] [--per-month n] | plan delete <name>Request limits of a plan.
sutra gateway firewall [--allow "10.0.0.0/8,192.168.1.5"] [--deny "203.0.113.9"]Addresses allowed and refused; with no options, shows them.
sutra gateway openapiOpenAPI of the deployed services (JSON).

Remote: --server <url> --token <token> (or SUTRA_SERVER, SUTRA_ADMIN_TOKEN). The token is a system account's API token (limited to its roles) or the server's SUTRA_ADMIN_TOKEN.

Exit code 0 = success, 1 = failure, 2 = wrong usage.

Examples

sutraflow setup                               install and build
sutraflow start                               the studio, in the background
sutraflow start engine                        a second engine on the same database
sutraflow status                              what runs, where, on which database
sutraflow cli sutras list                     deployed Sutras with their runs today
sutraflow cli runs list --status failed       failed runs
sutraflow cli user add meera --role developer --password-from-env NEW_PASSWORD
sutraflow db copy --to postgres://postgres@127.0.0.1:5432/sutraflow
sutraflow stop all                            graceful: running steps finish first
sutra package --project Shop --version 1.4.0 --out shop-1.4.0.sutra
sutra deploy shop-1.4.0.sutra --server https://prod:4800 --token $SUTRA_TOKEN
Guidelines

Run sutraflow stop before db copy, so nothing changes while the data is copied.
Give scripts a system account and its API token (sutra user add --system, sutra token create) rather than the local admin token.

23. The Admin Console

The Admin Console manages what is deployed: running projects and Sutras, approvals, engines, people, system accounts, roles and the audit log. Designing stays in the designer. Open it with Admin Console in the designer's top bar, or at /admin on the admin port (http://127.0.0.1:4800/admin). Headless engines serve the console too, without the designer.

Operate

  • Overview: tiles for engines, deployed Sutras, runs of the last 24 hours, waiting approvals, the work queue and the gateway certificate, and the latest failed runs with Resubmit. Test runs from the designer are not counted.
  • Applications: every deployed project with its package version and its Sutras: version, started or stopped, what starts it (REST path, SOAP path, timer, skill), runs of the last day and the last run. Stop makes the Sutra's triggers start nothing (its address answers 404, timers and listeners pause) while it stays deployed; Start brings it back on every engine; Restart does both at once, so its address, timers and listeners start fresh with the current connections. Runs opens its runs with every step's result, Resubmit and Cancel run; Versions deploys an earlier version; Tuning sets how the Sutra runs (below); Package history rolls the project back to an earlier package.
  • Approvals: running Sutras waiting for a person, with a comment and Approve or Reject.
  • Engines: every engine sharing the database: alive or silent, leader, steps running, heartbeat. Drain and stop asks one engine to finish its steps, hand the rest to the others and stop; your service manager starts it again. Delete old runs now runs housekeeping at once. Tuning on the same page sets engine values (below).

The Console panel and commands for every action

Console in the top bar opens a panel with every action taken in this browser tab: what was done, whether it worked, how long it took, and the server's answer. Each entry also shows the same action as a command, for Windows PowerShell and for Linux and macOS shells: the sutra command and the HTTP call (Invoke-RestMethod or curl). Every confirmation has Run it from a shell instead with the same commands, so an action can be scripted, put in a runbook, or tried again from a shell when the console is not at hand. Commands read the server address and token from SUTRA_SERVER and SUTRA_ADMIN_TOKEN; use a system account's API token. Passwords never appear in commands: they read NEW_PASSWORD from the environment.

sutra sutras list
sutra sutras restart "Order lookup API" --project "Orders"
sutra runs list --status failed
sutra runs resubmit 3f2c...
sutra approvals approve 42 --comment "checked"
sutra engines drain engine-2

Tuning

Tuning changes how deployed Sutras run, while they run. Every engine applies a change within a heartbeat, without a restart. Values set by environment variables stay the defaults, and an empty field returns to them.

Engine tuningWhat it does
Steps at onceSteps one engine runs at the same time. Set for all engines, or for one engine (a bigger machine, or 0 for a studio that should not run work).
Steps per run limitStops runs that take more steps, such as loops that never end.
Reply waitHow long REST, SOAP and MCP callers wait for a reply step.
Keep finished runs, Keep audit entriesDays before housekeeping deletes them.
Trace samplingShare of runs sent to the OpenTelemetry collector.
Sutra tuningWhat it does
Runs at onceMore runs wait as queued and start, oldest first, when one ends. Protects a slow partner system or a database.
PrioritySteps of higher priority Sutras are taken from the shared work queue first.
Run time limitRuns still open after this many minutes are cancelled with an error.
Retries, First retry afterFor steps whose own settings have no retries.
Step data in historyall, errors only (step data is kept only for runs that did not finish well), or none (for personal or bulky data).
Keep finished runsDays for this Sutra, instead of the engine setting.

Sutra tuning applies to every run of the deployed Sutra, whatever started it: REST or SOAP request, timer, file, mailbox, queue, MCP skill, channel or the Run API. A Sutra with several triggers shares one limit. Test and debug runs from the designer are not tuned, and runs started by Call Sutra always start (they count toward the limit, but never wait behind their own caller). Sutra tuning stays when a new version is deployed. Tuned Sutras show tuned in Applications.

Alerts

The Overview shows open alerts, runs of the last day and gateway traffic as charts. Under Alerts:

  • Channels say where alerts go: email through any project's SMTP connection, a webhook (a JSON POST with event, text and alert; chat tools that read a text field show the message; optionally signed with X-Sutra-Signature from a vault secret), or a deployed Sutra that starts with the alert as its input, to open a ticket or call someone. Send a test tries a channel.
  • Alert rules say what to watch: failed runs (of one Sutra or any), slow runs, gateway error rate, gateway latency (p95), engines (one stopped beating, or fewer alive than needed), work waiting in the queue too long, approvals waiting too long, the gateway certificate ending soon, listeners in error. Each rule has a severity (warning or critical), channels, whether to tell when it resolves, and reminders every few minutes while nobody acknowledged it. Check now shows what the rule finds at this moment.
  • Alerts lists what is open, newest first, and the history. The cluster leader checks every rule every 30 seconds, so a cluster alerts once; one alert per rule stays open until its condition clears. Acknowledge says someone is on it and stops reminders; Resolve closes it by hand. Each alert shows what was sent where, and whether it arrived.
sutra alerts                 (open alerts; exit code 1 while a critical alert is firing)
sutra alerts ack <id>
sutra alerts test "Operations team"

Gateway: apps, keys, plans, firewall, traffic

  • Apps and keys: an app is a consumer of your APIs (a partner, a mobile app, a team) with scopes such as orders:read and a plan. Create keys for it; each is shown once. Callers send a key in X-API-Key, or exchange it for an access token at POST /oauth/token on the gateway (client credentials: the app id and a key). Disabling an app or revoking a key refuses its calls at once.
  • To protect a service with apps, give its API security policy the authentication apps and the Required scopes.
  • Plans: requests per minute, hour and day and a monthly quota. All engines count together; over a limit the caller gets 429 with Retry-After, and every answer carries X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining.
  • Firewall: addresses or ranges the whole gateway allows or denies.
  • Traffic: requests over time (answered, refused, errors), latency p50/p95/p99, the busiest and slowest services, apps, status codes, and the request log with every request's caller, time and error.
  • APIs: what is served, with its policy; OpenAPI for the REST services, and the options to publish it at /openapi.json and to keep the request log.
sutra gateway plan set Partner --per-minute 120 --per-day 50000
sutra gateway app add "Acme shop" --scopes "orders:read" --plan Partner
sutra gateway key create "Acme shop" --name production --expires-days 365
sutra gateway stats --period 24h

Users, system accounts and roles

  • Users are people. An administrator adds them with a first password (Generate makes a strong one); by default they choose their own at the first sign-in. Five wrong passwords lock an account for 15 minutes; Unlock ends it sooner. Disable ends the person's sessions at once and keeps everything; Sign out everywhere ends sessions only.
  • System accounts are for engines, CI pipelines and API callers. They do not sign in to the designer. They get API tokens for the admin API, shown once and stored only as a hash, with an expiry and a Revoke button. A system account with a password can call gateway services whose API security policy accepts system accounts.
  • Roles are sets of permissions. A role is granted for all projects or for one project, and an account can hold several. Built-in roles: Administrator, Developer, Deployer, Operator, Approver, Viewer and API caller. New role combines permissions differently.
PermissionAllows
ViewSee the project, its Sutras, connections, runs and logs.
DesignEdit Sutras, schemas and project settings; test and debug runs.
ConnectionsAdd and change connections and API security policies.
DeployDeploy and undeploy Sutras, deploy packages, roll back, edit the deployment config.
OperateStart, stop, cancel and resubmit; clear runtime variable values.
ApproveDecide approvals.
Call servicesSystem accounts: call the project's gateway services with Basic sign-in.
Secrets, Engines, Gateway, Server settings, Users and roles, Audit, Alerts (channels, rules, acknowledging)Server permissions: they only come with a grant on all projects.
Always one administrator

Nobody can disable or delete their own account, and the last active administrator cannot lose the role.

Audit log

Every change, sign-in and refused request is recorded with who, when, from which address, what and the result, and with where it happened:

  • Where: the server (production, test or development, from SUTRA_ENVIRONMENT) and the engine, and whether it was a designer test run or a deployed Sutra.
  • Project and Sutra: name and id. The names are kept with the entry, so a renamed or deleted Sutra still reads as it was.

Filter by server, project, Sutra (choose the project first), person, result, words and dates; Export CSV saves what the filters show, with all these columns. Passwords, secret values and tokens are never recorded. Entries recorded before this version show no server.

Audit retention and clearing

The Retention card at the top of the Audit page shows how many entries there are, the oldest, and when the log was last cleared and by whom. With the Audit settings and clearing permission (Administrators have it):

  • Keep entries (days): housekeeping deletes older entries; 0 keeps everything. The default is SUTRA_AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS (365).
  • Delete older entries now, Clear before a date, or Clear all, each after a confirmation.

Clearing is recorded as an entry of its own (who, what, how many), so the log always shows that it was cleared. From a shell: sutra audit retention 180, sutra audit clear --before 2026-01-01.

The first administrator of a headless engine

A headless engine has no first-start page, so nobody who reaches it can claim it. Add the first administrator on the server, then sign in at /admin:

sutra user add admin --role administrator --password-from-env ADMIN_PASSWORD
sutra user add ci-orders --system --role deployer --project "Orders"
sutra user list

24. Running in production: engines, Docker, clusters

Headless engines

The same program started with SUTRA_MODE=engine runs Sutras without the studio: no designer pages and no editing. It keeps /health, /ready and /metrics, the Admin Console at /admin for its users, and an automation API for API tokens (the admin token or system account tokens). Packages in SUTRA_DEPLOY_DIR are deployed when it starts; a package that cannot be deployed stops the start.

Docker

docker build -t sutraflow:1.0.0 .
docker run -e SUTRA_MODE=engine -e SUTRA_ADMIN_TOKEN=... -e SUTRA_MASTER_KEY=... \
           -v ./deploy:/deploy:ro -p 8080:8080 sutraflow:1.0.0

The image runs as a non-root user, checks its own health, and writes JSON logs. docker-compose.yml has a studio and an engine; docker-compose.cluster.yml has PostgreSQL, a studio and two engines.

Clusters

Several engines share one database (SUTRA_DB=postgres://...), each with its own SUTRA_ENGINE_ID and all with the same SUTRA_MASTER_KEY.

  • Work is shared, and each step is run by exactly one engine.
  • One engine leads and runs timers and folder, mailbox, queue and Drive listeners, so they fire once. If it stops, another takes over within a few heartbeats.
  • Steps of an engine that stopped are finished by another.
  • Callers get their replies from whichever engine they reached.
  • A deploy reaches every engine.

Engines with SUTRA_WORKERS=0 only serve APIs. sutra status or GET /api/engine/status lists the engines, the leader and the queue.

Stopping without losing work

On docker stop, Ctrl+C or POST /api/engine/drain, an engine:

  1. reports not ready, so load balancers stop sending it requests;
  2. hands leadership over;
  3. lets running steps finish for SUTRA_DRAIN_MS, and hands the rest back to the queue for another engine;
  4. closes.

Monitoring

WhatWhere
Liveness and readiness/health, /ready on the admin port
Metrics/metrics (Prometheus): runs, steps by outcome, retries, durations, gateway requests, queue, leader, listeners
TracesSet OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT: each run is a trace with a span per step, continuing a caller's traceparent
LogsSUTRA_LOG_FORMAT=json: one JSON line per event on standard output, plus each project's log file

Runs

Finished runs older than SUTRA_RUN_RETENTION_DAYS (30 by default) are deleted; waiting runs are kept. A failed run can continue with Run again from the failed step in Runs: the failed step runs again with the same input, and the earlier steps' results are kept.

Checklist

  1. Set SUTRA_MASTER_KEY from your secret store, the same on every engine.
  2. Keep the studio on 127.0.0.1 or behind a VPN. Expose only the engines' gateway ports, behind a load balancer pointed at /ready.
  3. Set a long SUTRA_ADMIN_TOKEN; give it only to the release pipeline.
  4. Set the gateway certificate and require HTTPS in every API policy.
  5. Put environment-specific values in the deployment config, with ${env:NAME} for anything secret or host-specific.
  6. Release with packages; keep the files, they are your rollback.
  7. Back up the database (or the data folder).

The full operations guide is docs/deployment.md in the SutraFlow folder.

25. Troubleshooting

SymptomCause and remedy
A mapping shows not runThe activity was on a branch that was not taken in the last test. Test with data that takes that branch.
An API caller waits a minute, then gets 504A branch ended without Send HTTP response or SOAP reply. Add replies on every branch, including error branches.
A timer or file trigger does nothingOnly the deployed version listens. Deploy, then check the listeners table in Server & APIs.
Required fields not mappedThe Input tab names them. Map them, or remove the requirement from the schema.
Formula errorThe preview under the formula names the problem: an unknown function, a missing bracket, or a quote not doubled.
The run stops after 10000 stepsA loop that never ends. Check the condition that leaves it.
Let's Encrypt failsPort 80 on the domain must reach the gateway's HTTP port.

26. Activity reference

Triggers

▶Manual start

Palettes → Triggers · activity type start · trigger

Starts the Sutra from the studio or the Run API, with a test payload.

In scope
  • Starting a process from the studio (Test, Debug) or from another system through the Run API.
  • A test payload in JSON, and an optional payload schema that describes it for mapping.
Out of scope
  • Starting on a schedule, a request, a file or a message: use the trigger made for it.

When to use it

  • A process that another process or system starts on demand.
  • Building and testing a process before you choose its real trigger.

When to choose another activity

  • Run on a schedule → use Timer.
  • Expose the process as a REST API → use REST service.

Procedure

  1. Drag Manual start onto an empty canvas (a new flow already has one).
  2. In the General tab, write a test payload in JSON.
  3. Optionally pick a payload schema, so later steps see its fields in the mapper.

Output

  • The payload: either what the Run API sent, or the test payload.

Outputs (ports)

out

Settings reference

General tab

SettingWhat it doesValuesDefault
Payload schemaOptional. Describes the payload for mapping in later steps.A shared schema—
Test payload (JSON)Code or JSON{ "orderId": "A-1001" }

Also has the Settings tab every activity shares: retries, timeout, skip and breakpoint.

⏱Timer

Palettes → Triggers · activity type timer · trigger

Starts the Sutra on a schedule while the Sutra is deployed: a cron expression or a fixed interval.

In scope
  • Cron expressions with optional seconds and a time zone.
  • A fixed interval in seconds.
  • A fixed payload added to every run, plus firedAt.
Out of scope
  • Missed runs while the server was stopped are not run afterwards.
  • Calendars of holidays: test the date in an If / else after the timer.

When to use it

  • Nightly exports, polling an API every few minutes, a daily report.

When to choose another activity

  • React to new files instead of polling → use File trigger.
  • React to queue messages → use Message subscriber.

Procedure

  1. Choose cron or interval.
  2. For cron, write the expression, for example 0 30 9 * * MON-FRI, and the time zone.
  3. Deploy the Sutra. The timer runs only while the deployed version is active.

Output

  • The payload fields and firedAt (ISO date and time).
Guidelines
  • Put the schedule in a project variable ({{gv.EXPORT_CRON}}) so operations can change it per environment.

Outputs (ports)

out

Settings reference

General tab

SettingWhat it doesValuesDefault
Schedule bycron, intervalcron
Cron expression when Schedule by is cronSeconds field optional. Example: 0 30 9 * * MON-FRIText; {{gv.X}}, {{ev.X}} or an = formula0 */15 * * * *
Every (seconds) when Schedule by is intervalA number; may be a formula or variable300
Time zone when Schedule by is cronText; {{gv.X}}, {{ev.X}} or an = formulaAsia/Kolkata
Payload (JSON)Code or JSON{}

Also has the Settings tab every activity shares: retries, timeout, skip and breakpoint.

⇲REST service

Palettes → Triggers · activity type restService · trigger

Exposes the Sutra as an HTTP/REST API on the gateway. Reply with a Send HTTP response step.

In scope
  • One HTTP method and path per trigger, with :name path parameters.
  • An API security policy: Basic, API key, JWT, mutual TLS, IP allow list, rate limit, CORS.
  • JSON, XML, form and text bodies; a body schema for mapping.
Out of scope
  • Several paths in one trigger: use one REST service per path, or a path parameter.
  • Validation of the body against the schema (use Validate fields).

When to use it

  • Publishing a Sutra as an API for partners, apps and other systems.

When to choose another activity

  • Publish a SOAP web service with a WSDL → use SOAP service.
  • Receive work from a queue instead of HTTP → use Message subscriber.

Procedure

  1. Choose the method and the path, for example GET /orders/:id.
  2. Pick an API security policy (Resources → API security policy).
  3. Write a test request so you can test without a caller.
  4. End each branch with Send HTTP response.
  5. Deploy. The API is served by the gateway on ports 8080 and 8443.

Output

  • method, path, params, query, headers, body, auth (the caller after the policy check) and client (IP address, HTTPS).
Guidelines
  • Never deploy without a policy outside testing.
  • Always reply on the error branch too, or the caller waits until the reply timeout (60 seconds by default).

Outputs (ports)

out

Settings reference

General tab

SettingWhat it doesValuesDefault
MethodGET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, ANYPOST
PathUse :name for path parameters. Served on the gateway ports.Text; {{gv.X}}, {{ev.X}} or an = formula/orders/:id
API security policyEmpty = no authentication (not advised outside testing).A API security policy from Resources—
Max body size (KB)A number; may be a formula or variable1024
Request body schemaOptional. Shape of the JSON or XML body callers send.A shared schema—
Test request (JSON)Code or JSON{ "method": "POST", "params": { "id": "A-1001" }, "query": {}, …

Also has the Settings tab every activity shares: retries, timeout, skip and breakpoint.

⧉SOAP service

Palettes → Triggers · activity type soapService · trigger

Exposes the Sutra as a SOAP web service with a generated WSDL. Each operation is an output; reply with a SOAP reply step.

In scope
  • A SOAP 1.1 or 1.2 service with a generated WSDL at ?wsdl.
  • One output per operation, listed in the operations field.
  • The same API security policies as REST, plus WS-Security UsernameToken.
Out of scope
  • Importing an existing WSDL to define the service contract.
  • WS-Security encryption of incoming messages.

When to use it

  • Replacing or fronting a SOAP service that partners already call.

When to choose another activity

  • Publish JSON over HTTP → use REST service.
  • Call someone else's SOAP service → use Invoke SOAP service.

Procedure

  1. Name the service and namespace, and the path (for example /soap/orders).
  2. List the operations, separated by commas. Each becomes an output port.
  3. Connect each operation to its steps and end each with SOAP reply.
  4. Deploy, then give callers https://host:8443/soap/orders?wsdl.

Output

  • operation, body (the operation element as data), header, soapAction, auth, client.

Outputs (ports)

GetOrder CreateOrder The outputs follow your settings; shown here with the defaults.

HTTP / REST

⇋Send HTTP request

Palettes → HTTP / REST · activity type httpRequest

Calls a REST/HTTP API with headers, query, body and an outbound security profile (Basic, Bearer, API key, OAuth 2.0). TLS and client certificates come from the HTTP connection.

In scope
  • Any method, URL, query and headers; JSON, XML, text, form or a body mapped to a schema.
  • Outbound security: Basic, Bearer, API key, OAuth 2.0 client credentials, custom headers.
  • TLS and mutual TLS, proxy and timeout from an HTTP connection.
Out of scope
  • SOAP calls: use Invoke SOAP service, which builds the envelope and WS-Security.
  • Accounts that need a person to sign in (Google, Dropbox): use Connected API call.

When to use it

  • Calling REST APIs.

When to choose another activity

  • Call a SOAP service → use Invoke SOAP service.
  • Call an API of a connected OAuth account → use Connected API call.

Procedure

  1. Pick an HTTP connection (base URL, TLS) and outbound security, both from Resources.
  2. Choose the method and the URL; add query parameters and headers.
  3. Choose the body type and fill in the body, or map it to a schema in the Input tab.
  4. Pick a response schema so later steps see the response fields.
  5. Choose when the step fails, and connect the error output.

Output

  • status, headers, body (parsed JSON or XML when possible), ms.
Guidelines
  • Use retries in the Settings tab for calls that may fail briefly.

Outputs (ports)

out error
