■End

Palettes → Flow control · activity type end

Ends a branch and records its result. Can also stop the whole Sutra at once, as succeeded or failed, cancelling the other branches.

In scope
  • Ending a branch and recording its result.
  • Stopping the whole Sutra at once, as succeeded or failed: other branches still running or waiting are cancelled.
Out of scope
  • Replying to an API caller: use Send HTTP response or SOAP reply first.

When to use it

  • this branch: the normal end of a path.
  • Sutra: success: the work is done and nothing else should run, for example after a duplicate is detected.
  • Sutra: error: stop everything and mark the run failed, for example on an error output when no recovery is possible.

When to choose another activity

  • Fail a branch so an error handler can catch it → use Throw error.

Procedure

  1. Choose what ends: this branch, Sutra: success or Sutra: error.
  2. For Sutra: error, write the error message; it appears as the run's error in Runs and in the log.
  3. Connect it after the last step, or to an error output.

Output

  • The result, recorded as the run's output.

⤷Call Sutra

Palettes → Flow control · activity type callProcess

Runs another Sutra of this project with the input you give it and, when Wait is on, continues with its result (set by its Return activity). Build a piece of logic once and call it from many Sutras.

In scope
  • Running another Sutra of the same project with an input you set or map, and continuing with its result.
  • Waiting for the result, or starting it and continuing at once.
  • The draft while testing, the deployed version when deployed.
Out of scope
  • Sutras of other projects.
  • More than 10 levels of Sutras calling Sutras.

When to use it

  • Logic used by several Sutras: customer lookup, address cleaning, sending a standard alert.
  • Breaking a large Sutra into readable parts.

When to choose another activity

  • Signal other processes without waiting → use Send to channel.

Procedure

  1. Build the called Sutra: a Manual start (with a payload schema) and a Return at the end.
  2. In the calling Sutra, add Call Sutra and choose the Sutra.
  3. Set the input as a value, or choose mapping and map it to the payload schema in the Input tab.
  4. Optionally pick a result schema, so later steps see the result's fields.
  5. Connect the error output: a failure inside the called Sutra arrives there.

Output

  • With Wait on: the called Sutra's Return result. With Wait off: runId, process, started.
Guidelines
  • A called run appears in Runs as its own run with source sutra.
  • Deploy the called Sutra before the calling one, or deployed calls fail with "not deployed".

Outputs (ports)

out error

Out of scope
  • Replying to an API caller: use Send HTTP response or SOAP reply.

When to use it

  • The end of a Sutra that other Sutras call with Call Sutra.

When to choose another activity

  • End without a result, or stop as failed → use End.

  1. Choose value (for example {{input}}) or mapping with a result schema.

  • The result, returned to the calling Sutra and stored as the run's result.

⚠Error handler

Palettes → Flow control · activity type catch

Runs when any activity fails and its own error output is not connected. Other branches stop; the handler's path decides how the run ends (End with process: error to mark it failed). One per process.

In scope
  • One error handler per Sutra, started by the engine when an activity fails and its own error output is not connected.
  • The error (message, activity name and type, time) and the failed activity's input.
Out of scope
  • Errors already handled by a connected error output.
  • Errors inside the handler's own path: those fail the run.

When to use it

  • A common way to log, alert and clean up for every activity of a Sutra, instead of wiring each error output.

When to choose another activity

  • Handle one activity's error differently → use Throw error.

Procedure

  1. Drag Error handler onto the canvas. It has no input connection.
  2. Connect its output to the steps to run on an error, for example Log and Send email.
  3. End the path with End: Sutra: error marks the run failed; otherwise the run counts as handled and ends as done.

Output

  • error (message, step, type, at) and input, the failed activity's input.
Guidelines
  • When the handler starts, the Sutra's other branches stop.

Outputs (ports)

out

Also has the Settings tab every activity shares: retries, timeout, skip and breakpoint.

○No operation

Does nothing and passes its input on. A placeholder while you design, or a joining point for connections.

In scope
  • Passing the input on unchanged.
Out of scope
  • Waiting for branches: use Merge.

When to use it

  • A placeholder for an activity you have not chosen yet; a point where several connections meet.

Procedure

  1. Drag it in and connect it.

Output

  • The input, unchanged.

out error

Also has the Settings tab every activity shares: retries, timeout, skip and breakpoint.

Files

🗀File trigger

Palettes → Files · activity type fileTrigger · trigger

Starts the Sutra when a file in a folder is added, modified or removed (polling while the Sutra is deployed). Can read the file as text or as structured rows.

In scope
  • A folder with a wildcard pattern (*.csv, orders-*.xml), optionally with sub-folders.
  • Added, modified and removed events, each its own output.
  • Reading the file: text, CSV rows or lines typed by a schema, JSON, XML or base64, in the chosen encoding.
Out of scope
  • Remote folders: use Remote file trigger for SFTP and FTP.
  • Google Drive: use Google Drive / Docs trigger.

When to use it

  • Processing files dropped by another system or by people.

When to choose another activity

  • Read a file at a point in a Sutra → use Read file.
  • Sutra every file already in a folder → use List / read directory.

Procedure

  1. Enter the folder, for example {{gv.INBOX}}, and the pattern.
  2. Tick the events you need; each becomes an output.
  3. Set stable for seconds so files still being copied are not read early.
  4. Choose how to read the content. For CSV, pick a row schema to get typed, repeating rows.
  5. Move or delete the file at the end with Move / copy / delete file, so it is not picked up again after a restart.

Output

  • event and the file details (name, path, relativePath, folder, extension, size, modifiedAt), plus the content fields of the chosen format.

Outputs (ports)

added modified removed

⎙Write file

SFTP / FTP

⇣Remote file trigger

Palettes → SFTP / FTP · activity type remoteTrigger · trigger

Starts the Sutra for each new file in a folder on an SFTP or FTP server (polling while deployed). After a successful run the file is deleted, moved, or left and remembered.

In scope
  • A folder on an SFTP or FTP server, checked every few seconds for files matching a pattern.
  • Only files whose size stopped changing, so uploads still running are not read early.
  • After a successful run: move the file to a folder, delete it, or leave it and remember it.
  • Reading the file as text, CSV rows, lines, JSON, XML or base64.
Out of scope
  • Servers that push events: the trigger polls.
  • Local folders: use File trigger.

When to use it

  • Files a partner, bank or supplier drops on their server or yours.

When to choose another activity

  • List or read at a point in a Sutra → use List remote files.
  • Read one file → use Read remote file.

Procedure

  1. Pick the protocol and the SFTP or FTP connection.
  2. Enter the folder (inside the connection's base folder) and the pattern, for example *.csv.
  3. Choose what happens after the run. Move to a folder keeps a copy; Leave and remember never touches the partner's files.
  4. Choose how to read the content, then deploy.

Output

  • The file details (name, path, relativePath, size, modifiedAt, server) and the content fields of the chosen format.

out

⛭SQL script

Palettes → DB Ops · activity type dbScript

Runs an install or change script: CREATE DATABASE, CREATE TABLE, CREATE PROCEDURE, seed rows. Statements are separated by a line with only ";" and run one after another, not in one transaction: most databases keep table and procedure changes at once.

In scope
  • An install or change script: CREATE DATABASE, CREATE TABLE, CREATE PROCEDURE, seed rows.
  • Statements separated by a line with only ;, run one after another, so procedure bodies may hold their own semicolons.
  • Stopping at the first failure, or running the rest and listing the failures.
Out of scope
  • All-or-nothing changes to data: use SQL transaction. Most databases keep table and procedure changes at once anyway.

When to use it

  • Setting up the tables and procedures a Sutra needs, on a new server or in a test.

Procedure

  1. Pick the connection.
  2. Write the script; put a line with only ; between statements.
  3. Use IF NOT EXISTS and DROP ... IF EXISTS so the script can run again.
  4. Choose what happens when a statement fails.

Output

  • results (one per statement, with ok and error), ran and failed.

out error

⇩Message subscriber

Palettes → Service Bus · activity type busSubscribe · trigger

Starts the Sutra for each message on a queue or topic while deployed. Gives the body, the JMS headers and the custom properties. Acknowledge automatically, after the Sutra succeeds, or with a Confirm message activity.

In scope
  • Queues and topics, selectors, durable subscriptions, Kafka consumer groups.
  • Acknowledgement: auto (on receipt), client (after the run succeeds) or explicit (Confirm message).
  • On failure: requeue, or dead-letter after a number of redeliveries; concurrency.
Out of scope
  • Exactly-once processing: design steps so a message processed twice does no harm.

When to use it

  • Processing work from a queue, reacting to events.

Procedure

  1. Choose the broker, connection and destination.
  2. Choose the acknowledgement mode; client suits most Sutras.
  3. Choose what happens on failure and how many messages run at once.
  4. Write a test message so you can test without a broker.
  5. Deploy; the subscriber runs while the deployed version is active.

Output

  • body, headers (JMS headers), properties, destination, redelivered.

Outputs (ports)

out

Scripts (PowerShell, shell)

❯PowerShell script

Palettes → Scripts (PowerShell, shell) · activity type powershell

Runs a PowerShell script on the server and captures its output, error output and exit code. Values come in as environment variables. Needs scripts to be allowed in Server & APIs.

In scope
  • A PowerShell script on the server: Windows PowerShell 5.1 or PowerShell 7.
  • Values as environment variables ($env:NAME) and the previous step's output as a JSON file ($env:SUTRA_INPUT_FILE).
  • Output, error output, both together in order, the exit code, and JSON output read as data.
Out of scope
  • Scripts that wait for someone to type: they run without a console.
  • Running on another machine: use PowerShell remoting inside the script.

When to use it

  • Windows administration: services, files, event logs, Active Directory, IIS, scheduled tasks.

When to choose another activity

  • Logic on data without touching the server → use JavaScript code.
  • A program with arguments, no script → use Run program.

Procedure

  1. Ask an administrator to tick Allow script activities in Server & APIs.
  2. Choose Windows PowerShell or PowerShell 7.
  3. Add the values the script needs under Variables, for example ORDER_ID = {{input.orderId}}, and read them as $env:ORDER_ID.
  4. Write the script. End with ... | ConvertTo-Json to hand data to the next step.
  5. Connect the error output: it carries the exit code, the output and the error output.

Output

  • exitCode, stdout (output), stderr (error output), output (both, in the order printed), lines, json (when the output is JSON), ms, timedOut, truncated (output over 5 MB). On the error output, the same under {input.error.details}.
Guidelines
  • Never paste values into the script text; use Variables. Data from a request or a file then cannot become commands.
  • Scripts run with the rights of the account SutraFlow runs as: give that account only what the scripts need.

Outputs (ports)

out error

✺AI agent

Palettes → AI · activity type aiAgent

Works towards a goal in steps: thinks, picks a tool, uses it, looks at the result, until it can answer. Tools are Sutras with an AI tool trigger, a knowledge base and the tools of an MCP server. Keeps the conversation in an AI memory store. Waits for tool Sutras without holding a worker, and never repeats a finished tool after a restart.

In scope
  • A goal or a message worked on in steps: the model thinks, picks a tool, uses it, reads the result, and repeats until it can answer.
  • Tools: Sutras that start with AI tool, the knowledge base (search_knowledge), and the tools of an MCP client connection.
  • Memory per session in an AI memory store, fitted to the context window; passages from a knowledge base before the first step.
  • Limits on steps, tokens and time; outputs done, needs a person and limit reached.
Out of scope
  • Decisions that must always go one way, such as refunds: route them with If / else before the agent; small models do not reliably choose to ask.
  • Streaming the answer word by word.

When to use it

  • An order desk, a support assistant, an internal helper that looks things up in several systems.

When to choose another activity

  • One question answered from documents only → use Ask knowledge.
  • One fixed prompt → use AI prompt.

Procedure

  1. Pick the AI provider and write the instructions: who the agent is, what it may do, the tone.
  2. Set the message (usually {{input.message}}) and, for conversations, an AI memory store and the session id.
  3. Choose the tools: all AI tools of the project, chosen ones, or none; add a knowledge base or an MCP client.
  4. Set the limits, and connect needs a person to Ask a person and limit reached to a reply.

Output

  • answer (done), question (needs a person) or reason (limit reached); steps with each tool, input, result or error; toolCalls, tokens, session and ai.
Guidelines
  • A tool Sutra runs as a called Sutra: the agent waits without holding a worker, and after a restart it continues without running a finished tool again.
  • Messages of one session are handled one at a time, in arrival order; other sessions run alongside.
  • Small local models (phi4-mini) handle look-ups well; give them few tools and clear instructions.

Outputs (ports)

done needs a person limit reached error

⧉Call MCP tool

Palettes → AI · activity type mcpCall

Lists the tools of another MCP server, or calls one with arguments: a file system, GitHub, a database, a search engine, another SutraFlow. The tool reporting an error goes to "tool error".

In scope
  • Listing the tools of another MCP server, or calling one with arguments, over HTTP or a command started on this server.
Out of scope
  • Giving the tools to an AI agent: set the MCP client on the agent instead.

When to use it

  • A file system, GitHub, a database or search engine that has an MCP server; another SutraFlow.

Procedure

  1. Create an MCP client connection under Resources.
  2. Use list tools once to see the names, then call a tool with its arguments as JSON.

Output

  • result, text and isError; for list, tools. A tool error goes to tool error.

☄Agent channel

Palettes → AI · activity type agentChannel · trigger

Publishes the Sutra as an agent while it is deployed, at several entry points at once: a chat page and chat API, an OpenAI-compatible API (model = agent name), a tool on an MCP server (Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, Antigravity, Cursor) and an A2A agent. Every message arrives the same way; answer with Agent reply.

In scope
  • Publishing the Sutra as an agent while it is deployed, at several entry points: chat page and chat API (with a chat button for any web page), OpenAI-compatible API, a tool on an MCP server, and A2A.
  • A security policy per entry point, and an answer time after which callers get a job id.
Out of scope
  • Messaging apps (Slack, Teams, WhatsApp): use their webhooks with a REST service that hands off to the agent.

When to use it

  • An agent people chat with on your site, that Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot or Antigravity call as a tool, and that other agents call over A2A.

Procedure

  1. Give the agent a name (it becomes the addresses) and a description.
  2. Tick the entry points and set who may use each.
  3. Build the work, usually AI guard then AI agent, and end every branch with Agent reply.
  4. Deploy. Server & APIs lists the addresses.

Output

  • message, sessionId, channel (chat, openai, mcp, a2a, handoff, test), caller and history.

out

⛉AI guard

Palettes → AI · activity type aiGuard

Checks text before it goes to a model or out to a person: hides personal data, catches instructions hidden in text an agent reads (prompt injection), blocks topics and checks length or JSON shape. Optionally asks a model as well.

In scope
  • Hiding personal data (emails, phone numbers, cards, IBAN, Aadhaar, PAN), catching hidden instructions, blocking topics, checking length and JSON shape.
  • Optionally a model as a second opinion.
Out of scope
  • A full content moderation service.

When to use it

  • Before an agent reads what a customer or a web page wrote; before an answer goes out.

Procedure

  1. Set the text and tick the checks.
  2. List blocked topics, one per line.
  3. Connect pass to the work and blocked to a polite reply.

Output

  • text with personal data hidden, original, hidden, findings and reason.

pass blocked error

✧AI tool

Palettes → AI · activity type mcpTool · trigger

Makes the Sutra a tool: the AI agents of this project can use it, and, while deployed, AI assistants such as Claude can call it over the Model Context Protocol at the gateway address /mcp. Describe what it does and what it needs; end the Sutra with Reply to AI.

In scope
  • Making a Sutra a tool: the AI agents of this project use it, and AI assistants such as Claude call it over the Model Context Protocol while it is deployed.
  • A name, a title and a description the AI reads; inputs as rows or a JSON schema; an optional result schema.
  • An MCP server to group skills under one address, and an API security policy.
Out of scope
  • Calling other MCP servers from a Sutra: use Call MCP tool.
  • Streaming partial results.

When to use it

  • Letting an assistant do real work through your Sutras: write a CSV file, post to a Facebook page, look up an order, raise a ticket.

When to choose another activity

  • Expose the Sutra to programs instead of AI assistants → use REST service.

Procedure

  1. Create an MCP server under Resources (address such as /mcp/orders, instructions, security policy), or leave the server empty to use /mcp.
  2. Drag MCP skill onto a new Sutra and choose the server.
  3. Give a tool name and a description that says what it does, when to use it and what it returns.
  4. List the inputs: one row each, with a description; start it with number:, array: and so on for other types, and optional: when it may be left out.
  5. Tick Changes data when it creates, changes or deletes something.
  6. End every branch with Reply to AI, and Deploy.

Output

  • arguments (what the AI sent), tool, auth (the caller after the policy check) and client.
Guidelines
  • The description is what the AI chooses by: write it for a person who has never seen the Sutra.
  • A skill that changes data should be confirmed by the user; assistants do so when Changes data is ticked.

28. Function reference

123 functions for formulas and mappings, grouped as in the mapper's function library. Names ignore case.

String

FunctionWhat it doesExample
concat(a, b, ...)Joins text values.concat('Name : ', {input.name})
substring(text, start, length?)Part of the text; start counts from 1.substring('ABCDEF', 2, 3) = 'BCD'
substring-before(text, find)Text before the first match.substring-before('a@b.com', '@') = 'a'
substring-after(text, find)Text after the first match.substring-after('a@b.com', '@') = 'b.com'
substring-before-last(text, find)Text before the last match.
substring-after-last(text, find)Text after the last match.substring-after-last('a/b/c.txt', '/') = 'c.txt'
upper-case(text)Upper case.
lower-case(text)Lower case.
trim(text)Removes spaces at both ends.
left-trim(text)Removes leading spaces.
right-trim(text)Removes trailing spaces.
normalize-space(text)Trims and collapses inner spaces.
string-length(text)Number of characters.
contains(text, find)True when text contains find.
starts-with(text, prefix)True when text starts with prefix.
ends-with(text, suffix)True when text ends with suffix.
index-of(text, find)Position of find (1-based), 0 when absent.
replace(text, find, with)Replaces every occurrence (plain text).
replace-regex(text, pattern, with)Regular expression replace; $1 refers to groups.
matches(text, pattern)True when the regular expression matches.
translate(text, from, to)Replaces characters one for one.
pad(text, length, char?)Pads on the right.
pad-front(text, length, char?)Pads on the left, e.g. leading zeros.pad-front(42, 6, '0') = '000042'
tokenize(text, separator)Splits text into a list.
string-join(list, separator)Joins a list into text.
capitalize(text)First letter of each word upper case.

Conversion

FunctionWhat it doesExample
xs:string(value)Converts to text (objects become JSON).
xs:integer(value)Whole number (fraction dropped); error when not a number.
xs:int(value)Same as xs:integer.
xs:long(value)Same as xs:integer.
xs:decimal(value)Decimal number; error when not a number.
xs:double(value)Floating-point number (NaN when not a number).
xs:float(value)Same as xs:double.
xs:date(value)Date as YYYY-MM-DD.
xs:dateTime(value)Date and time as ISO 8601.
xs:time(value)Time as HH:mm:ss.
xs:boolean(value)Converts to true/false ("true", "1" and "yes" are true).

Encode/Decode

FunctionWhat it doesExample
string-to-base64(text)Base64 encode.
base64-to-string(base64)Base64 decode.
url-encode(text)Encode for URLs.
url-decode(text)Decode URL encoding.
hex-encode(text)Text to hexadecimal.
hex-decode(hex)Hexadecimal to text.
escape-xml(text)Escape < > & ' " for XML.
unescape-xml(text)Undo XML escaping.
md5(text)MD5 hash (hex).
sha1(text)SHA-1 hash (hex).
sha256(text)SHA-256 hash (hex).
hmac-sha256(key, text, encoding?)HMAC signature, hex or base64.
to-json(value)Data to JSON text.
from-json(text)JSON text to data.

Variables

FunctionWhat it doesExample
get-project-variable('NAME')Current value of a project variable (same as {gv.NAME}, but the name can be computed).
set-project-variable('NAME', value)Changes a project variable for every later run (kept until the next deployment config change). Returns the value.
get-sengine-variable('NAME')Sengine variable: a server setting made by the administrator in Server & APIs, shared by all projects. Read it; do not change it from Sutras.
set-sengine-variable('NAME', value)Changes a Sengine variable for every project. Not advised: works only when the administrator allows it in Server & APIs.

Utility

FunctionWhat it doesExample
newline()A line break, for concat().
tab()A tab character.
uuid()A new random id (UUID v4).
timestamp(date?)Milliseconds since 1970 (now when empty).timestamp() = 1791900000000
timestamp-seconds(date?)Seconds since 1970 (Unix time).
current-timestamp(format?, timezone?)Now as text; default 'YYYYMMDDHHmmssSSS', handy for file names and ids.concat('orders-', current-timestamp('YYYYMMDD-HHmmss'), '.csv')
random-string(length, characters?)Random letters and digits.
type-of(value)text, number, boolean, list, object or null.
hostname()Name of the server running the Sutra.
file-name(path)Last part of a path: C:\in\a.csv gives a.csv.
file-base-name(path)File name without its extension.
file-extension(path)Extension without the dot (csv).
dir-name(path)Folder part of a path.
path-join(a, b, ...)Joins path parts with one separator.path-join({gv.INBOX}, '*.csv')
format-bytes(bytes)Human size: 1536 gives 1.5 KB.
default(value, fallback)The value, or fallback when it is empty.
json-path(object, path)Reads a nested field by path text: json-path({input}, 'order.lines[0].sku').

Date/Time

FunctionWhat it doesExample
current-dateTime()Now, ISO 8601 (UTC).
current-date()Today as YYYY-MM-DD (server time zone).
current-time()Time now as HH:mm:ss.
format-date(format, date, timezone?)Formats a date. Tokens: YYYY YY MMMM MMM MM DD dddd ddd; text in [brackets] stays.format-date('DD-MM-YY', {input.date})
format-time(format, date, timezone?)Formats a time. Tokens: HH hh mm ss SSS A Z.format-time('hh:mm A', {input.at})
format-dateTime(format, date, timezone?)Formats date and time, e.g. in Asia/Kolkata.format-dateTime('DD MMM YYYY HH:mm', {now}, 'Asia/Kolkata')
parse-date(format, text)Reads a date written in the given format; returns ISO 8601.parse-date('DD/MM/YYYY', '31/12/2026')
add-to-date(date, years, months, days)Adds (or with negatives subtracts) years, months and days.
add-to-dateTime(date, years, months, days, hours, minutes, seconds)Adds to a date-time.
days-between(from, to)Whole days from one date to another.
year-from-date(date)Year number.
month-from-date(date)Month number 1 to 12.
day-from-date(date)Day of month.
from-timestamp(ms)Milliseconds since 1970 to ISO date.

Number

FunctionWhat it doesExample
number(value)Converts to a number (commas and currency signs removed).
round(number, decimals?)Rounds half up.
floor(number)Rounds down.
ceiling(number)Rounds up.
abs(number)Absolute value.
power(base, exponent)Base to the power.
format-number(number, pattern)Formats with a pattern such as '#,##0.00'.format-number(1234.5, '#,##0.00') = '1,234.50'
sum(list, field?)Total of a list, or of a field in each item.
avg(list, field?)Average.
min(a, b, ...) or min(list)Smallest value.
max(a, b, ...) or max(list)Largest value.
random(min, max)Random whole number between min and max.
is-number(value)True when the value is a number.

Logical

FunctionWhat it doesExample
if(condition, then, else)Chooses a value; only the chosen side is evaluated.if({input.qty} > 10, 'bulk', 'retail')
coalesce(a, b, ...)First value that is not empty.coalesce({input.mobile}, {input.phone}, 'n/a')
not(value)True when the value is false or empty.
equals-ignore-case(a, b)Case-insensitive comparison.

Sequence

FunctionWhat it doesExample
exists(value)True when the field is present (even if empty text).
empty(value)True when missing, empty text or an empty list.
last() or last(list)Inside a For-Each or [filter]: number of items; with a list: its last item.
position()Inside a For-Each or [filter]: position of the current item (from 1).{input.rows}[position() <= 10]
count(list)Number of items (0 when missing, 1 for a single value).
item-at(list, position)Item at a position (1-based).
first(list)First item.
distinct(list)Removes duplicates.

List

FunctionWhat it doesExample
pluck(list, field)Takes one field from every item.
sort(list, field?, descending?)Sorts a list.
filter-by(list, field, value)Items whose field equals value.
list(a, b, ...)Makes a list.
group-by(list, field)Groups items by a field: a list of { key, items, count }.group-by({input.orders}, 'customer')
count-by(list, field)How many items have each value: { value: count }.
flatten(list, childField?)Flattens nested lists; with a child field, one item per child carrying its parent as _parent.flatten({input.orders}, 'lines')
slice(list, start, count?)Part of a list; start counts from 1.
concat-lists(list, list, ...)Joins lists into one.
contains-item(list, value)True when the list holds the value.
object('key', value, 'key2', value2, ...)Builds an object from key/value pairs.
merge(object, object, ...)Combines objects; later fields win.

upperUpper case
lowerLower case
trimRemove spaces at both ends
numberConvert to a number

parseTurn JSON text into data
defaultdefault:"x" when empty

joinjoin:", "

addadd:10

base64Encode as Base64

urlencodeEncode for a URL

xmlescapeEscape for XML
